opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions can be quite misleading, and there are a couple of different regimes to think about.

In the near term, while AI tools are mostly speeding up parts of an engineer's work, like writing boilerplate, debugging, or navigating an unfamiliar codebase, you can get something like a Jevons paradox effect. Software gets cheaper to produce, so people want more of it. There's a huge backlog of software that would be valuable but isn't worth building at current costs. So demand for engineers might stay flat or even rise for a while, and the job shifts toward specifying what you want, reviewing outputs, and handling the parts the models still struggle with.

But I'd be cautious about extrapolating that too far, because it depends on there being some bottleneck that only humans can fill. At METR, a lot of what we try to measure is how long a task, measured in human time, AI agents can complete reliably, and that horizon has been growing fairly quickly, roughly doubling on the order of every several months. When the models can only do things that take a human a few minutes, they're a productivity tool. When they can reliably do tasks that take a human a day, a week, or a month, the picture changes. At that point it's less "engineers with better autocomplete" and more that whole projects can be delegated.

So the question becomes: what's left that humans uniquely provide? Maybe judgment about what to build, accountability, taste, coordinating with stakeholders. Those matter, but they're a much smaller share of engineering labour than people sometimes assume, and they're not obviously out of reach for models either.

I'd also add some humility about measurement. Benchmarks can overstate real-world usefulness because real tasks are messier, less well specified, and need more context. We've seen cases where developers felt sped up by AI tools but were measurably slower in practice. So the near-term effect is genuinely uncertain and probably smaller than the hype suggests in some settings. The longer-term trend line is the thing I'd pay attention to. If it continues, the effect on demand for human software engineers could be quite dramatic, and it could also feed back into AI development itself, which is part of why we care about tracking it so closely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI handling whole projects and the importance of human bottlenecks, but does not state that automating the occupation requires performing nearly all its constituent tasks.

r002.rationale: It says AI can speed up engineering work and that cheaper software may raise demand, but does not clearly say this makes human work more profitable through increased productivity.

r003.rationale: It names possible human contributions such as judgment and coordination, but does not suggest that humans may need to take on new kinds of tasks.

r004.rationale: The response mentions a Jevons paradox effect but gives no working-horse history or illustration of demand first rising and then collapsing after near-complete substitution.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's genuinely uncertain, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who sounds very confident in either direction. But let me try to lay out how I think about it.

The thing I'd push back on first is the framing where there's some fixed quantity of "software engineering work" and the question is just what fraction of it gets done by models versus humans. That's not how it's worked historically. Every time we've made programmers dramatically more productive, whether that's compilers, open source, cloud infrastructure, the amount of software people wanted went up, and the number of programmers went up with it. Demand for software has been pretty elastic. So in the near term, I'd expect something like that again: a lot of the automation shows up as people doing more ambitious things rather than fewer people doing the same things.

But I don't think you can just extrapolate that forever, and this is where my day job makes me a bit less sanguine than a lot of economists. At METR we try to measure what AI systems can actually do on realistic software and research engineering tasks, and the trend is quite steep. The length of task that models can complete autonomously, at a reasonable success rate, has been roughly doubling on a timescale of months, not years. If you take that seriously, you go from "models are a very good autocomplete" to "models can do a day of an engineer's work" to "models can do a week of work" in a fairly short window. And the previous waves of productivity tools never had that property. A compiler doesn't eventually learn to do the whole job.

So I'd separate two regimes. In the first one, which is where I think we are now, models complement engineers. They're great at well-specified, short-horizon stuff, bad at long-horizon work with messy context, and you still very much need a human who understands the system, decides what to build, and catches the ways the model is confidently wrong. In that regime I'd actually expect demand for good engineers to hold up or increase, though the mix of skills shifts a lot toward specification, review, and judgment, and away from typing out the code.

The second regime is one where the models are reliably better than most humans at essentially the whole loop, including the long-horizon parts. There I think the honest answer is that demand for human software engineers as a labor category drops a lot, and the comforting historical analogies mostly stop applying. I don't know when that happens, but I don't think it's unreasonable to put meaningful probability on it within this decade, which is a very different claim than "software jobs are safe."

One thing I'd add, because I think people underweight it: our measurements suggest the gap between what models can do in a benchmark and what they can do in the real world is still substantial. Realistic tasks have ambiguous goals, missing context, and no clean success signal. Models do noticeably worse there than on things like competitive programming. So when someone says "the model solved this hard problem, engineers are done," I'd want to know how much hand-holding was involved and whether anyone checked that the solution was actually what was wanted. That gap is real, it's just also closing, and I'd rather people plan for it closing than assume it's permanent.

r001.rationale: It says demand would drop substantially if models became better than humans at “essentially the whole loop,” including long-horizon work.

r002.rationale: It links productivity gains to increased demand for software and programmers, but does not explain that automating a small fraction of tasks makes human work more profitable.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that humans would need to take on new kinds of tasks to remain economically relevant after AI can perform current software engineering tasks.

r004.rationale: It discusses past productivity tools such as compilers, but does not use working horses to illustrate an initial rise in labor demand followed by collapse under near-complete substitution.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two effects pulling in opposite directions. One is that, if AI can do more of the work, you need fewer human hours to produce a given piece of software. The other is that software becomes cheaper to produce, so people want more of it. Projects that weren’t previously worth doing become worthwhile.

So automating, say, half of a software engineer’s tasks doesn’t straightforwardly mean you need half as many software engineers. You could end up employing more people, if demand expands enough and humans are still needed for important parts of the process.

But I wouldn’t assume that continues indefinitely. The crucial question is whether humans remain a necessary complement to the AI. If you still need someone to specify the problem, check the result, and coordinate the work, increased demand for software could increase demand for those people. If AI can also do those things, then demand for software could grow enormously without creating much demand for human engineers.

So I’d distinguish between AI making engineers more productive and AI being able to substitute for them across the whole job. Those can have very different effects on employment.

r001.rationale: It says AI may substitute for engineers “across the whole job,” distinguishing that from merely making them more productive.

r002.rationale: It describes fewer human hours per piece of software, but does not say automating a small fraction of tasks makes human work more profitable through increased productivity.

r003.rationale: It names specifying, checking, and coordinating as tasks humans may still do, but does not suggest humans may need to take on new kinds of tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not use working horses or any historical example of demand rising before near-complete labor substitution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between demand for software and demand for human software engineers. If AI makes software much cheaper to produce, people will want more of it. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll want more human engineers, because the additional work could also be done by AI.

For a while, you could have a situation where AI automates some tasks and makes the remaining human work more valuable. Engineers can build more ambitious things, and projects that weren’t economical before become worthwhile. Whether that increases hiring depends on how much demand expands and how much human involvement each project still needs.

If AI can do essentially the whole job, though, I don’t think increased demand for software is enough to protect demand for human labor. You need some reason that a human remains a useful input. So I’d be cautious about taking productivity gains today as evidence that employment will stay high as the systems become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says that if AI can do “essentially the whole job,” increased software demand may not protect human labor, communicating that near-complete automation is needed for occupational automation.

r002.rationale: It says automating some tasks can make remaining human work more valuable, but does not clearly explain that this happens by increasing human productivity.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that humans may need to take on new kinds of tasks to remain economically relevant.

r004.rationale: It does not use working horses or another historical example of temporary labor demand growth followed by collapse under near-complete substitution.
